title: A route remembered
bodyMd:
When the fictional poet Sela returned to her childhood town, she described the walk from the station to her former home without naming a single street. The route proceeds by sounds: a gate striking a wall, a pump handle falling, the change in footsteps beneath an arch. Critics initially praised the poem as an exact recovery of a vanished place. Yet the route cannot be followed on the town plan printed beside the poem in its first edition. One turn leads into a courtyard that had been closed before Sela was born. The accompanying plan was not a later editorial addition that readers could dismiss as an accidental distraction. Its presence in the first edition made the relationship between route and map part of the work as initially encountered. A reader could move back and forth between the two, discovering that the confidence of the poem's sensory detail did not yield a usable itinerary. The discrepancy invited interpretation rather than merely correcting a mistake. It asked what kind of accuracy a literary return might claim when it did not claim the accuracy of a guidebook.

This mismatch need not be treated as a failure of memory. The poem repeatedly shifts between what the speaker hears now and what she expects to hear. At the pump, she pauses for a sound that does not arrive. Beneath the arch, the footsteps belong first to the returning adult and then, grammatically without announcement, to a child running ahead. The route is organized by anticipated recognition rather than by navigable distance.

The closed courtyard is especially important. Family stories had placed a grandmother's workshop there, and the poem reaches it through a description Sela could have inherited rather than witnessed. The town is thus remembered through more than personal experience. It includes a transmitted geography: places made familiar by repeated stories even when physically inaccessible.

The poem does not ask readers to choose between a true map and a false recollection. The printed plan establishes the mismatch that makes its other organization visible. Documentary geography and remembered geography answer different questions. One tells a traveler how to arrive; the other shows how a speaker becomes attached to places she has seen, lost, expected, or only been told about. The poem's precision lies in distinguishing those modes of belonging, not in giving reliable directions.
